kp.k: Professional upheaval undermined established sociological approaches
kp.d: Gorman and Sandefur describe a mid-20th-century golden age for both professional work and its sociological study. They argue that dramatic changes affecting professions in the 1970s and 1980s made older research approaches inadequate, leaving the research area quiescent. This is a historical interpretation presented in the supplied abstract; the full text and its supporting evidence are not captured.
qs: Both professional work and the sociological study of professional work experienced a "golden age" in the mid-20th century.
When dramatic changes began to shake the professions in the 1970s and 1980s, however, old approaches no longer fit, and the research area became quiescent.

kp.k: Research persisted across disciplinary fields under different names
kp.d: The authors qualify the apparent decline of the sociology of professions: interest in professional work did not disappear but continued under other labels across sociological and interdisciplinary fields. Their essay seeks to bring these dispersed research streams together.
qs: Yet interest in professional work simply "went underground," surfacing under other names in a variety of sociological and interdisciplinary fields.

This essay brings these disparate research streams together and shows that they cohere around four central themes: expert knowledge, autonomy, a normative orientation grounded in community, and high status, income, and other rewards.

kp.k: The research focus broadened beyond traditional professions
kp.d: The authors identify a shift in the object of study from traditional professions alone to a wider range of expert or knowledge-based occupations. The claim concerns the scope of professional-work research, rather than AI-driven changes in legal services, which the supplied material does not discuss.
qs: In the process, researchers' focus expanded to include a broader range of "expert" or "knowledge-based" occupations as well as traditional professions.

kp.k: Four themes unify research on knowledge-based work
kp.d: The essay proposes four organising themes connecting the dispersed literature: expert knowledge, autonomy, a community-grounded normative orientation, and rewards including high status and income. These constitute the authors' conceptual synthesis of professional and knowledge-based work, not a reported measurement of changes in particular occupations.
